contrast.note: The perfect would present the whole period as one result.

sense.label: simple past or perfect?
sense.why: A period that is not over yet takes the perfect: 'heb ... gefietst'.

clauses.text: Ik heb deze week elke dag gefietst
clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'heb' is second; 'deze week' and 'elke dag' follow and the participle 'gefietst' ends the clause.

pat-tense-72.meaning: I have cycled every day this week.
pat-tense-72.order: 'Deze week' is a period that includes the present, so the perfect is the natural tense. Fietsen takes hebben as an activity.
pat-tense-72.compare: English 'I have cycled every day this week' uses the same perfect. Dutch also does.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb deze week elke dag fietsen.
mistakes.right: Ik heb deze week elke dag gefietst.
mistakes.why: The perfect needs the participle 'gefietst', not the infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: Ik ben deze week elke dag gefietst.
mistakes.right: Ik heb deze week elke dag gefietst.
mistakes.why: As an activity 'fietsen' takes hebben. (not "Ik ben deze week elke dag gefietst.", but "Ik heb deze week elke dag gefietst.")

contrast.dutch: Ik fietste vorige week elke dag.
contrast.english: I cycled every day last week.
contrast.note: A finished week takes the simple past. Compare: Ik fietste vorige week elke dag.

sense.label: simple past or perfect?
sense.why: A state in the past takes the simple past of zijn: 'was'.

clauses.text: Het was heel druk op kantoor
clauses.subject: Het
clauses.why: 'Het' is first, so the past 'was' is second; the predicate 'heel druk' and the place follow.

pat-tense-73.meaning: It was very busy at the office.
pat-tense-73.order: The simple past of zijn describes a past state without an auxiliary. 'Heel' stands before the adjective 'druk'.
pat-tense-73.compare: English 'it was very busy' is the same. Dutch needs no auxiliary. For this card: "Het was heel druk op kantoor".

mistakes.wrong: Het wasde heel druk op kantoor.
mistakes.right: Het was heel druk op kantoor.
mistakes.why: 'Zijn' is irregular: the past is 'was'. (not "Het wasde heel druk op kantoor.", but "Het was heel druk op kantoor.")

mistakes.wrong: Het was druk heel op kantoor.
mistakes.right: Het was heel druk op kantoor.
mistakes.why: The degree word 'heel' goes before the adjective.

contrast.dutch: Het is heel druk geweest op kantoor.
contrast.english: It has been very busy at the office.
contrast.note: The perfect links the busy time to now. Compare: Het is heel druk geweest op kantoor.

sense.label: simple past or perfect?
sense.why: A day that is still going takes the perfect of zijn: 'is geweest'.

clauses.text: Het is vandaag heel druk geweest op kantoor
clauses.subject: Het
clauses.why: 'Het' is first, so 'is' is second; 'vandaag' and the predicate follow and the participle 'geweest' ends the verb pair.

pat-tense-74.meaning: It has been very busy at the office today.
pat-tense-74.order: 'Vandaag' is a period that includes the present, so the perfect 'is geweest' links it to now. The place phrase follows the participle.
pat-tense-74.forms: zijn > geweest (zijn). Card: "Het is vandaag heel druk geweest op kantoor".
pat-tense-74.compare: English 'it has been busy today' uses the same perfect. Dutch also does.

mistakes.wrong: Het is vandaag heel druk gewees op kantoor.
mistakes.right: Het is vandaag heel druk geweest op kantoor.
mistakes.why: The participle of 'zijn' is 'geweest', never 'gewees'.

mistakes.wrong: Het heeft vandaag heel druk geweest op kantoor.
mistakes.right: Het is vandaag heel druk geweest op kantoor.
mistakes.why: 'Zijn' takes zijn as auxiliary. (not "Het heeft vandaag heel druk geweest op kantoor.", but "Het is vandaag heel druk geweest op kantoor.")

contrast.dutch: Het was gisteren heel druk op kantoor.
contrast.english: It was very busy at the office yesterday.
contrast.note: A finished day takes the simple past. Compare: Het was gisteren heel druk op kantoor.

sense.label: perfect with prefix verbs
sense.why: Voorbereiden is separable: the participle 'voorbereid' joins the particle and has no ge-.

clauses.subject: Zij
clauses.why: Zij is first, so 'heeft' is second; the object follows and the participle 'voorbereid' ends the clause.

pat-tense-75.order: The separable verb joins its particle in the participle. Because 'bereiden' begins with be-, there is no ge-. Read it as "Zij heeft de lessen voorbereid".
pat-tense-75.compare: English 'has prepared' is one word. Dutch builds one participle. For this card: "Zij heeft de lessen voorbereid".

mistakes.wrong: Zij heeft de lessen voorgebereid.
mistakes.why: 'Bereiden' starts with be-, so there is no ge-: 'voorbereid'.

mistakes.wrong: Zij heeft de lessen bereid voor.
mistakes.why: The particle joins the participle. (not "Zij heeft de lessen bereid voor.", but "Zij heeft de lessen voorbereid.")

contrast.note: The present splits the verb. Compare: Zij bereidt de lessen voor.

sense.label: perfect with prefix verbs
sense.why: Aankomen is a movement verb, so the perfect uses zijn; the participle is 'aangekomen'.

clauses.text: De trein is te laat aangekomen
clauses.subject: De trein
clauses.why: 'De trein' is first, so 'is' is second; 'te laat' follows and the participle 'aangekomen' ends the clause.

pat-tense-76.order: The particle 'aan' sits inside the participle. 'Te laat' stands before it. Read it as "De trein is te laat aangekomen".
pat-tense-76.compare: English 'arrived late' is a simple past. Dutch reports it with the perfect.

mistakes.wrong: De trein heeft te laat aangekomen.
mistakes.right: De trein is te laat aangekomen.
mistakes.why: 'Aankomen' takes zijn. (not "De trein heeft te laat aangekomen.", but "De trein is te laat aangekomen.")

mistakes.wrong: De trein is aan gekomen te laat.
mistakes.right: De trein is te laat aangekomen.
mistakes.why: Particle and participle are one word: 'aangekomen'. (not "De trein is aan gekomen te laat.", but "De trein is te laat aangekomen.")

contrast.dutch: De trein kwam te laat aan.
contrast.note: The simple past splits the verb. Compare: De trein kwam te laat aan.

sense.label: perfect with prefix verbs
sense.why: Beantwoorden is inseparable (be-): the participle has no ge-.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'heb' is second; the object follows and the participle 'beantwoord' ends the clause.

pat-tense-77.order: 'Beantwoorden' has the unstressed prefix be-, so no ge- is added to the participle. Read it as "Ik heb de e-mail beantwoord".
pat-tense-77.compare: English 'have answered' is two words. Dutch has no ge-. For this card: "Ik heb de e-mail beantwoord".

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb de e-mail gebeantwoord.
mistakes.why: After the prefix be- the participle has no ge-: 'beantwoord'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb de e-mail antwoord.
mistakes.why: The participle keeps its prefix: 'beantwoord'.

contrast.note: The present keeps the verb whole. Compare: Ik beantwoord de e-mail.

sense.label: perfect with prefix verbs
sense.why: Ontdekken is inseparable (ont-): the participle has no ge-.

clauses.subject: Hij
clauses.why: Hij is first, so 'heeft' is second; the object follows and the participle 'ontdekt' ends the clause.

pat-tense-78.order: The prefix ont- is unstressed and inseparable, so the participle has no ge-. Read it as "Hij heeft de fout ontdekt".
pat-tense-78.compare: English 'has discovered' is two words. Dutch has no ge-. For this card: "Hij heeft de fout ontdekt".

mistakes.wrong: Hij heeft de fout geontdekt.
mistakes.why: After the prefix ont- the participle has no ge-: 'ontdekt'.

mistakes.wrong: Hij is de fout ontdekt.
mistakes.why: 'Ontdekken' takes hebben. (not "Hij is de fout ontdekt.", but "Hij heeft de fout ontdekt.")

contrast.note: The simple past narrates the find. Compare: Hij ontdekte de fout.

sense.label: perfect with prefix verbs
sense.why: Verkopen is inseparable (ver-), strong, and has no ge-: 'verkocht'.

clauses.subject: Wij
clauses.why: Wij is first, so the plural 'hebben' is second; the object follows and the participle 'verkocht' ends the clause.

pat-tense-79.order: The prefix ver- is unstressed, so there is no ge-. The verb is irregular: verkopen, verkocht. Read it as "Wij hebben de auto verkocht".
pat-tense-79.compare: English 'have sold' is two words. Dutch has no ge-. For this card: "Wij hebben de auto verkocht".

mistakes.wrong: Wij hebben de auto geverkocht.
mistakes.why: After the prefix ver- the participle has no ge-: 'verkocht'.

mistakes.wrong: Wij hebben de auto verkoopt.
mistakes.why: 'Verkopen' is irregular: the participle is 'verkocht'.

contrast.note: The simple past narrates the sale. Compare: Wij verkochten de auto.

sense.label: perfect with prefix verbs
sense.why: Verliezen is inseparable (ver-) and strong: 'verloren'.

clauses.subject: Zij
clauses.why: Zij is first, so 'heeft' is second; the object follows and the participle 'verloren' ends the clause.

pat-tense-80.order: The strong participle 'verloren' has no ge-. 'Haar werk' means her job here. Read it as "Zij heeft haar werk verloren".
pat-tense-80.compare: English 'has lost' is two words. Dutch has no ge-. For this card: "Zij heeft haar werk verloren".

mistakes.wrong: Zij heeft haar werk geverloren.
mistakes.why: After the prefix ver- the participle has no ge-: 'verloren'.

mistakes.wrong: Zij heeft haar werk verliesd.
mistakes.why: 'Verliezen' is strong: the participle is 'verloren'.

contrast.note: The simple past narrates the loss. Compare: Zij verloor haar werk.

sense.label: perfect with prefix verbs
sense.why: Ontvangen is inseparable (ont-): the participle equals the infinitive.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'heb' is second; the object follows and the participle 'ontvangen' ends the clause.

pat-tense-81.order: The participle 'ontvangen' looks like the infinitive, because the prefix ont- takes no ge-. Read it as "Ik heb het pakket ontvangen".
pat-tense-81.compare: English 'have received' is two words. Dutch participle equals the infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb het pakket geontvangen.
mistakes.why: After the prefix ont- the participle has no ge-: 'ontvangen'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik ben het pakket ontvangen.
mistakes.why: 'Ontvangen' takes hebben. (not "Ik ben het pakket ontvangen.", but "Ik heb het pakket ontvangen.")

contrast.note: The simple past narrates the delivery. Compare: Ik ontving het pakket.

sense.label: perfect with prefix verbs
sense.why: Herkennen is inseparable (her-): the participle has no ge-.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'heb' is second; the object follows and the participle 'herkend' ends the clause.

pat-tense-82.order: The prefix her- is unstressed and inseparable, so the participle is 'herkend'. Read it as "Ik heb de fout herkend".
pat-tense-82.compare: English 'have recognised' is two words. Dutch has no ge-. For this card: "Ik heb de fout herkend".

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb de fout geherkend.
mistakes.why: After the prefix her- the participle has no ge-: 'herkend'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb de fout herkent.
mistakes.why: The participle of 'herkennen' ends in -d: 'herkend'.

contrast.note: The simple past narrates the moment. Compare: Ik herkende de fout.

sense.label: perfect with a modal
sense.why: A modal in the perfect uses two infinitives at the end instead of a participle: 'heb ... moeten werken'.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'heb' is second; 'gisteren' follows and the two infinitives 'moeten werken' end the clause.

pat-tense-83.order: With a modal verb the perfect uses the infinitive 'moeten' where you would expect 'gemoeten'. The two infinitives close the clause.
pat-tense-83.compare: English 'had to work' is a simple past. Dutch builds a perfect with two infinitives.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb gisteren gemoeten werken.
mistakes.why: In the perfect a modal stays an infinitive: 'moeten werken'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik ben gisteren moeten werken.
mistakes.why: The modal perfect takes hebben. (not "Ik ben gisteren moeten werken.", but "Ik heb gisteren moeten werken.")

contrast.note: The simple past gives the same obligation.

sense.label: perfect with a modal
sense.why: With a modal the standard auxiliary is hebben, even if the main verb alone would take zijn.

clauses.subject: Zij
clauses.why: Zij is first, so 'heeft' is second; 'niet' follows and the infinitives 'kunnen komen' end the clause.

pat-tense-84.order: With a modal the auxiliary is hebben even if the main verb alone would take zijn. 'Niet' stands before the infinitive group.
pat-tense-84.compare: English 'could not come' is a simple past. Dutch builds the perfect with two infinitives.

mistakes.wrong: Zij is niet kunnen komen.
mistakes.why: With a modal the auxiliary is hebben. (not "Zij is niet kunnen komen.", but "Zij heeft niet kunnen komen.")

mistakes.wrong: Zij heeft niet gekund komen.
mistakes.why: In the perfect a modal stays an infinitive: 'kunnen komen'.

contrast.note: The simple past states the same fact. Compare: Zij kon niet komen.

sense.label: perfect with a modal
sense.why: The modal perfect again with hebben: 'hebben ... moeten wachten'.

clauses.subject: We
clauses.why: We is first, so the plural 'hebben' is second; 'lang' follows and the infinitives 'moeten wachten' end the clause.

pat-tense-85.meaning: We had to wait a long time.
pat-tense-85.order: The adverb 'lang' stands before the two infinitives. The plural 'we' needs 'hebben'. Read it as "We hebben lang moeten wachten".
pat-tense-85.compare: English 'had to wait a long time' is a simple past. Dutch builds a perfect.

mistakes.wrong: We hebben lang gemoeten wachten.
mistakes.why: In the perfect a modal stays an infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: We hebben moeten lang wachten.
mistakes.why: The adverb 'lang' goes before the infinitives.

contrast.english: We had to wait a long time.
contrast.note: The simple past gives the same obligation. Compare: We moesten lang wachten.

sense.label: perfect with a modal
sense.why: The modal perfect with 'willen': 'heeft ... willen proberen'.

clauses.text: Hij heeft het nog eens willen proberen
clauses.subject: Hij
clauses.why: Hij is first, so 'heeft' is second; the object and 'nog eens' follow and the infinitives 'willen proberen' end the clause.

pat-tense-86.meaning: He wanted to try it once more.
pat-tense-86.order: 'Willen' stays an infinitive in the perfect. 'Nog eens' (once more) stands before the infinitives. Read it as "Hij heeft het nog eens willen proberen".
pat-tense-86.compare: English 'wanted to try' is a simple past. Dutch builds a perfect. For this card: "Hij heeft het nog eens willen proberen".

mistakes.wrong: Hij heeft het nog eens gewild proberen.
mistakes.right: Hij heeft het nog eens willen proberen.
mistakes.why: In the perfect a modal stays an infinitive: 'willen proberen'.

mistakes.wrong: Hij heeft nog eens het willen proberen.
mistakes.right: Hij heeft het nog eens willen proberen.
mistakes.why: The object 'het' goes before 'nog eens'. (not "Hij heeft nog eens het willen proberen.", but "Hij heeft het nog eens willen proberen.")

contrast.dutch: Hij wilde het nog eens proberen.
contrast.english: He wanted to try it once more.
contrast.note: The simple past gives the same wish. Compare: Hij wilde het nog eens proberen.

sense.label: perfect with a modal
sense.why: 'Gaan' plus infinitive in the perfect takes zijn and two infinitives: 'ben ... gaan wandelen'.

clauses.text: Ik ben vanmiddag even gaan wandelen
clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'ben' is second; 'vanmiddag even' follows and the infinitives 'gaan wandelen' end the clause.

pat-tense-87.meaning: I went for a short walk this afternoon.
pat-tense-87.order: 'Gaan wandelen' (to go for a walk) is a combination of two infinitives. In the perfect it takes zijn and stays as two infinitives.
pat-tense-87.compare: English 'went for a walk' is a simple past. Dutch builds a perfect with zijn.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb vanmiddag even gaan wandelen.
mistakes.right: Ik ben vanmiddag even gaan wandelen.
mistakes.why: 'Gaan wandelen' takes zijn in the perfect.

mistakes.wrong: Ik ben vanmiddag even gegaan wandelen.
mistakes.right: Ik ben vanmiddag even gaan wandelen.
mistakes.why: In the perfect 'gaan' stays an infinitive: 'gaan wandelen'.

contrast.english: I went for a short walk this afternoon.
contrast.note: The simple past narrates the same break. Compare: Ik ging vanmiddag even wandelen.

sense.label: perfect in a dependent clause
sense.why: In a dependent clause the auxiliary 'heeft' stands before the participle 'gelezen' at the end.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'weet' is second; the dependent clause tells what is known. The clause is "Ik weet". (2) (3) (4) (5) (6)

clauses.text: dat hij het verslag heeft gelezen
clauses.subject: hij
clauses.why: In the dependent clause the subject 'hij' comes first, then the object, and the verb group 'heeft gelezen' ends the clause with the finite 'heeft' before the participle.

pat-tense-88.meaning: I know that he has read the report.
pat-tense-88.order: In a main clause the perfect would read 'Hij heeft het verslag gelezen' with the pair around the object. In the dependent clause the object stays before the pair, and the verb group closes the clause.
pat-tense-88.forms: lezen > gelezen (hebben). The order 'heeft gelezen' is the standard one; 'gelezen heeft' also occurs.
pat-tense-88.compare: English 'that he has read the report' keeps 'has read' together after the subject. Dutch puts the verb group last.

mistakes.wrong: Ik weet dat hij heeft het verslag gelezen.
mistakes.right: Ik weet dat hij het verslag heeft gelezen.
mistakes.why: In a dependent clause the verb group goes to the end, behind the object.

mistakes.wrong: Ik weet dat hij het verslag gelezen.
mistakes.right: Ik weet dat hij het verslag heeft gelezen.
mistakes.why: The dependent clause needs its finite verb 'heeft'.

contrast.note: In a main clause the pair wraps the object.

sense.label: perfect in a dependent clause
sense.why: A dependent clause with zijn: 'is vertrokken' closes the clause.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'denk' is second; the dependent clause gives the opinion.

clauses.subject: zij
clauses.why: In the dependent clause the subject 'zij' comes first, then 'al', and the verb group 'is vertrokken' ends the clause with the finite 'is' before the participle.

pat-tense-89.meaning: I think she has already left.
pat-tense-89.order: The adverb 'al' (already) stands before the verb group. The participle 'vertrokken' closes the clause. Read it as "Ik denk dat zij al is vertrokken".
pat-tense-89.forms: vertrekken > vertrokken (zijn). Card: "Ik denk dat zij al is vertrokken".
pat-tense-89.compare: English 'that she has already left' keeps 'has left' together. Dutch puts the group last.

mistakes.wrong: Ik denk dat zij al is vertrok.
mistakes.right: Ik denk dat zij al is vertrokken.
mistakes.why: The participle of 'vertrekken' is 'vertrokken', with the ending -en.

mistakes.wrong: Ik denk dat zij is al vertrokken.
mistakes.right: Ik denk dat zij al is vertrokken.
mistakes.why: The verb group goes to the end of the dependent clause.

contrast.note: In a main clause the auxiliary is second.

sense.label: perfect in a dependent clause
sense.why: A dependent clause with 'niet': the negation stands before the verb group.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'zie' is second; the dependent clause says what is seen.

clauses.text: dat de klant niet is gekomen
clauses.subject: de klant
clauses.why: In the dependent clause the subject 'de klant' comes first, then 'niet', and the verb group 'is gekomen' ends the clause.

pat-tense-90.meaning: I see that the customer has not come.
pat-tense-90.order: The negation 'niet' stands before the verb group at the end of the dependent clause. Read it as "Ik zie dat de klant niet is gekomen".
pat-tense-90.compare: English 'that the customer has not come' keeps 'has not come' close to the subject. Dutch puts 'niet' and the group at the end.

mistakes.wrong: Ik zie dat de klant is niet gekomen.
mistakes.right: Ik zie dat de klant niet is gekomen.
mistakes.why: In a dependent clause 'niet' stands before the verb group.

mistakes.wrong: Ik zie dat de klant niet heeft gekomen.
mistakes.right: Ik zie dat de klant niet is gekomen.
mistakes.why: 'Komen' takes zijn. (not "Ik zie dat de klant niet heeft gekomen.", but "Ik zie dat de klant niet is gekomen.")

contrast.note: In a main clause the auxiliary is second. Compare: De klant is niet gekomen.

sense.label: perfect in a dependent clause
sense.why: The omdat-clause opens the sentence, so the main clause inverts: 'bleef ik thuis'.

clauses.subject: het
clauses.why: In the omdat-clause the dummy subject 'het' comes first, then 'gisteren', and the verb group 'heeft geregend' ends the clause.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The dependent clause fills slot one, so the main clause starts with its verb 'bleef' and the subject 'ik' follows.

pat-tense-91.meaning: Because it rained yesterday, I stayed at home.
pat-tense-91.order: The dependent clause has the perfect 'heeft geregend' at its end, and the main clause has the simple past 'bleef'. Mixing the two tenses is natural, because the rain is the reason and the staying home is the story.
pat-tense-91.compare: English 'because it rained yesterday, I stayed home' uses a simple past twice. Dutch often uses the perfect for the reason.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat het gisteren geregend heeft, ik bleef thuis.
mistakes.right: Omdat het gisteren heeft geregend, bleef ik thuis.
mistakes.why: After the opening clause the main clause starts with its verb: 'bleef ik'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat het gisteren regende, bleef ik thuis gisteren.
mistakes.right: Omdat het gisteren heeft geregend, bleef ik thuis.
mistakes.why: The time word belongs inside the dependent clause.

contrast.dutch: Ik bleef thuis omdat het gisteren heeft geregend.
contrast.english: I stayed at home because it rained yesterday.
contrast.note: With the main clause first there is no inversion.

sense.label: perfect in a dependent clause
sense.why: A dependent clause with a plural subject: 'hebben gewacht' closes the clause.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'weet' is second; the dependent clause tells what is known. The clause is "Ik weet". (2) (3) (4) (5) (6) (7)

clauses.subject: ze
clauses.why: In the dependent clause the subject 'ze' comes first, then 'lang', and the verb group 'hebben gewacht' ends the clause.

pat-tense-92.meaning: I know that they have waited a long time.
pat-tense-92.order: The adverb 'lang' stands before the verb group. The plural 'ze' needs the plural 'hebben'. Read it as "Ik weet dat ze lang hebben gewacht".
pat-tense-92.forms: wachten > gewacht (hebben). Card: "Ik weet dat ze lang hebben gewacht".
pat-tense-92.compare: English 'that they have waited a long time' keeps 'have waited' together. Dutch puts the group last.

mistakes.wrong: Ik weet dat ze lang heeft gewacht.
mistakes.right: Ik weet dat ze lang hebben gewacht.
mistakes.why: The plural 'ze' needs 'hebben'. (not "Ik weet dat ze lang heeft gewacht.", but "Ik weet dat ze lang hebben gewacht.")

mistakes.wrong: Ik weet dat ze hebben lang gewacht.
mistakes.right: Ik weet dat ze lang hebben gewacht.
mistakes.why: The verb group goes to the end of the dependent clause. (not "Ik weet dat ze hebben lang gewacht.", but "Ik weet dat ze lang hebben gewacht.")

contrast.english: They have waited a long time.
contrast.note: In a main clause the auxiliary is second. Compare: Ze hebben lang gewacht.

sense.label: perfect in a dependent clause
sense.why: A dependent clause with a joined particle: 'is uitgevallen' closes the clause.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'hoor' is second; the dependent clause gives the hearsay.

clauses.subject: de server
clauses.why: In the dependent clause the subject 'de server' comes first, then the verb group 'is uitgevallen' with the finite 'is' before the joined participle.

pat-tense-93.meaning: I hear that the server has gone down.
pat-tense-93.order: The particle 'uit' is part of the participle. Both the auxiliary and the participle end the dependent clause. Read it as "Ik hoor dat de server is uitgevallen".
pat-tense-93.compare: English 'that the server has gone down' keeps 'has gone down' together. Dutch puts the group last.

mistakes.wrong: Ik hoor dat de server uit is gevallen.
mistakes.right: Ik hoor dat de server is uitgevallen.
mistakes.why: The participle is one word: 'uitgevallen'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik hoor dat de server heeft uitgevallen.
mistakes.right: Ik hoor dat de server is uitgevallen.
mistakes.why: 'Uitvallen' takes zijn. (not "Ik hoor dat de server heeft uitgevallen.", but "Ik hoor dat de server is uitgevallen.")

contrast.note: In a main clause the auxiliary is second. Compare: De server is uitgevallen.

sense.label: past perfect
sense.why: The past perfect 'had ... gelezen' puts the reading before another moment in the past.

clauses.text: Ik had het rapport al gelezen
clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'had' is second; the object and 'al' follow and the participle 'gelezen' ends the clause.

pat-tense-94.meaning: I had already read the report.
pat-tense-94.order: The past perfect is the perfect shifted into the past: 'had' instead of 'heb'. 'Al' stresses that the reading came first.
pat-tense-94.compare: English 'had already read' uses the same shape. Dutch puts the object and 'al' between the auxiliary and the participle.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb het rapport al gelezen.
mistakes.right: Ik had het rapport al gelezen.
mistakes.why: The past perfect needs 'had' to put the event earlier in the past.

mistakes.wrong: Ik had het rapport al lezen.
mistakes.right: Ik had het rapport al gelezen.
mistakes.why: The past perfect needs the participle 'gelezen'.

contrast.dutch: Ik heb het rapport al gelezen.
contrast.english: I have already read the report.
contrast.note: The present perfect links the reading to now.

sense.label: past perfect
sense.why: The past perfect with zijn: 'was ... vertrokken'.

clauses.subject: Zij
clauses.why: Zij is first, so the past 'was' is second; 'al' follows and the participle 'vertrokken' ends the clause.

pat-tense-95.order: The auxiliary 'zijn' in the past is 'was', followed by the participle. 'Al' stresses that she left earlier. Read it as "Zij was al vertrokken".
pat-tense-95.compare: English 'she had already left' is the same. Dutch uses 'was ... vertrokken'.

mistakes.wrong: Zij had al vertrokken.
mistakes.why: 'Vertrekken' takes zijn: 'was vertrokken'.

mistakes.wrong: Zij is al vertrokken.
mistakes.why: The present perfect does not place the leaving before another past moment.

contrast.note: The present perfect links the event to now.

sense.label: past perfect
sense.why: The past perfect with hebben in the plural: 'hadden ... betaald'.

clauses.text: We hadden de bestelling al betaald
clauses.subject: We
clauses.why: We is first, so the plural past 'hadden' is second; the object and 'al' follow and the participle 'betaald' ends the clause.

pat-tense-96.meaning: We had already paid for the order.
pat-tense-96.order: The plural 'hadden' matches 'we'. 'Betaald' has no ge-, because of the prefix be-. Read it as "We hadden de bestelling al betaald".
pat-tense-96.compare: English 'we had already paid' is the same for all subjects. Dutch has 'had' and 'hadden'.

mistakes.wrong: We had de bestelling al betaald.
mistakes.right: We hadden de bestelling al betaald.
mistakes.why: The plural 'we' needs 'hadden'. (not "We had de bestelling al betaald.", but "We hadden de bestelling al betaald.")

mistakes.wrong: We hadden de bestelling al gebetaald.
mistakes.right: We hadden de bestelling al betaald.
mistakes.why: After the prefix be- the participle has no ge-: 'betaald'. (not "We hadden de bestelling al gebetaald.", but "We hadden de bestelling al betaald.")

contrast.dutch: We hebben de bestelling al betaald.
contrast.english: We have already paid for the order.
contrast.note: The present perfect links the payment to now.

sense.label: past perfect
sense.why: 'Weg zijn' in the past perfect is simply 'was weg': a state, not an action.

clauses.subject: De trein
clauses.why: 'De trein' is first, so the past 'was' is second; 'al weg' ends the clause.

pat-tense-97.order: Here no participle is needed: 'weg' is a predicate that names the state. The simple past of zijn plus 'al' already shows that the leaving came before.
pat-tense-97.forms: zijn: was. 'Weg zijn' = to be gone.
pat-tense-97.compare: English 'the train had already gone' uses a participle. Dutch uses the state 'weg'.

mistakes.wrong: De trein had al weg.
mistakes.why: 'Zijn' with a predicate takes 'was', not 'had'.

mistakes.wrong: De trein was weg al.
mistakes.why: 'Al' goes before the predicate. (not "De trein was weg al.", but "De trein was al weg.")

contrast.note: The present describes the state now. Compare: De trein is al weg.

sense.label: past perfect
sense.why: 'Nog niet' with the past perfect: the sending had not happened yet.

clauses.text: Hij had de brief nog niet gestuurd
clauses.subject: Hij
clauses.why: Hij is first, so the past 'had' is second; the object and 'nog niet' follow and the participle 'gestuurd' ends the clause.

pat-tense-98.meaning: He had not yet sent the letter.
pat-tense-98.order: 'Nog niet' (not yet) stands before the participle. The past perfect says that the sending had not happened by the moment you talk about.
pat-tense-98.compare: English 'had not yet sent' puts 'yet' at the end. Dutch puts 'nog niet' before the participle.

mistakes.wrong: Hij had de brief niet nog gestuurd.
mistakes.right: Hij had de brief nog niet gestuurd.
mistakes.why: The phrase is 'nog niet', not 'niet nog'.

mistakes.wrong: Hij had de brief nog niet sturen.
mistakes.right: Hij had de brief nog niet gestuurd.
mistakes.why: The past perfect needs the participle 'gestuurd'.

contrast.dutch: Hij heeft de brief nog niet gestuurd.
contrast.english: He has not yet sent the letter.
contrast.note: The present perfect speaks about now. Compare: Hij heeft de brief nog niet gestuurd.

sense.label: perfect in a question
sense.why: A yes/no question in the perfect starts with the auxiliary and ends with the participle.

clauses.subject: je
clauses.why: The auxiliary 'Heb' opens the yes/no question, then 'je' and the object, and the participle 'geschreven' ends the clause.

pat-tense-99.order: Questions invert auxiliary and subject. The participle stays at the end. With 'je' after the verb the auxiliary loses its -t.
pat-tense-99.compare: English 'Have you written the letter?' keeps 'written' close. Dutch puts the object between.

mistakes.wrong: Je hebt de brief geschreven?
mistakes.why: A real yes/no question starts with the auxiliary: 'Heb je'.

mistakes.wrong: Hebt je de brief geschreven?
mistakes.why: After the verb 'je' takes no -t: 'heb je'.

contrast.note: The statement puts the subject first. Compare: Je hebt de brief geschreven.
